title: Intelligent Fleet Throttle Orchestrator for SLA-driven Throughput Guarantees
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Summary: Build a fleet-level throttle orchestrator that enforces per-customer and per-route throughput guarantees while enabling safe autoscaling and graceful overload behavior. The orchestrator should be the authoritative decision point for admitting or shedding requests for Dedicated pools and must integrate with existing routing, autoscaler, and metrics layers.

Problem statement: Customers on Dedicated expect throughput SLAs (requests/sec or tokens/sec) with predictable tail latency. When demand spikes or capacity rebalancing happens, we need deterministic controls to honor commitments, avoid noisy neighbors, and keep overall latency within SLO bands. Current per-instance rate caps and ad-hoc queueing lead to unfairness, hotspots during rolling upgrades, and opaque shedding events.

Goals:
- Enforce guaranteed throughput budgets per customer/route and a configurable best-effort pool for burst traffic.
- Coordinate with autoscaling so admission decisions expose meaningful signals (e.g., when to scale, and when to shed).
- Provide graceful degradation (partial response, prioritized short-circuiting, model-fallback) rather than indiscriminate 503s.
- Emit telemetry suitable for SLO dashboards and billing reconciliation.
- Support canary rollout and per-customer overrides during migration.

Non-goals: global re-architecture of routing; changes to customer-facing API surface. This work lives inside Dedicated routing stack and control plane configs.

High-level design:
1) Budget manager: persistent token budgets (tokens/sec and burst) per customer/route derived from subscription SKU + free-burst policies. Budgets are stored in the control plane and periodically synced to fleet controllers.
2) Multi-tier token buckets at runtime: global fleet bucket -> pool bucket -> customer/route bucket. Admission checks consume from the deepest applicable bucket. If customer bucket exhausted, fall back to burst pool if allowed.
3) Queue with priority aging: short-lived per-shard queues (max wait configurable, default 200ms) with aging to avoid starvation. Priority is computed from customer SLA class, request timestamp, and cost-estimate (estimated tokens).
4) Overload shedding policies: soft-shed (return partial/compressed response or model-variant), hard-shed (503) with reason codes. Soft-shed hooks implemented as pluggable middleware for model routing.
5) Autoscaler integration: admission rejections and token depletion metrics feed the autoscaler. Autoscaler will consider sustained budget saturation (>30s) as a scaling signal.
6) Observability: expose token consumption, queue depth histograms, per-route shed counters, and backpressure latency percentiles.

APIs & Configs:
- Control-plane config: budget templates, burst pool size, priority weights, queue timeouts.
- Runtime: /admit endpoint (gRPC) that takes route key, estimated token cost and returns admit|enqueue|shed with reason and suggested fallback.
- Admin: per-customer override and emergency-eviction endpoints.

Compatibility & safety: default to conservative budgets during rollout. Configs are feature-flagged and can be disabled per-cluster. Backward compatible: if orchestrator is disabled, revert to per-instance caps.
acceptance_criteria: Authoritative admission decisions are made by orchestrator for all requests to Dedicated pools behind a feature flag.
Per-customer throughput budgets enforce guarantees in synthetic load tests (95th percentile match within 10% of target) and prevent noisy neighbor amplification.
Autoscaler receives clear saturation signals and triggers scale-ups during sustained budget exhaustion in canary tests.
Soft-shed behavior returns documented fallback responses and reduces hard 503s by >= 50% during overload scenarios.
Telemetry dashboards show token consumption, per-route queueing latency, and shed reasons; metrics ingestion validated against an internal dashboard template.
implementation_notes: Runtime should be implemented as a sidecar-capable admission service in Rust for low-latency checks. Use a compact in-memory token store with periodic control-plane reconciliation; persist long-lived budgets to Postgres for audit. Token consumption must be atomic and lock-free across shards (per-shard counters + vector clock reconciliation). Queue implemented with ring buffer per worker to avoid GC pauses. Expose structured logs with reason codes (THROTTLE_BUDGET, BURST_POOL_EXHAUSTED, QUEUE_TIMEOUT, AUTOSCALER_SATURATION). Add e2e benchmarking harness measuring admitted vs shed rates and tail latency under mixed workload profiles.
rollout_plan: Week 0: Merge feature-flagged orchestrator in staging; smoke tests with synthetic tenants.
Week 1: Canary to 5% of Dedicated fleet with conservative budgets; monitor token metrics and tail latency.
Week 2: Expand to 25% and enable soft-shed fallbacks for eligible routes.
Week 3: 100% rollout behind opt-in per-customer flags; validate autoscaler coupling.
Contingency: Immediate rollback via feature flag and backfill using per-instance caps if regressions > 5% error rate.
comments: 2026-02-11 - Asha Patel: Initial write-up and acceptance criteria. Punted some kernel-selection ideas to a follow-up ticket to keep scope focused.

2026-02-17 - Luis Gomez: Prototype admission gRPC endpoint working in local cluster. Observed ~0.7ms additional median latency in Rust sidecar; acceptable. Linking PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/routing/pull/432
2026-02-23 - Maya Chen (PM): Confirmed SLA mapping table; added customer tiers and burst allowances to the design doc. Requested runbook for emergency evictions.
2026-03-02 - Security review: no secrets introduced; recommended RBAC for admin override endpoints (done).

2026-03-09 - Reliability: ran mixed-load test with 40% burst traffic. Soft-shed reduced hard 503s by ~62% and allowed critical tenants to keep baseline throughput. Need to tune aging weight for low-SLA tenants.
2026-03-12 - Luis Gomez: Updated implementation notes to use per-shard counters and vector clock reconciliation. Preparing canary rollout config for Week 1.
